newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW - RBA cuts official rates to 5.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - RBA cuts official rates to 5.0 pct.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia cut official interest by 50 basis points to 5.0 percent on Wednesday.

The markets had been factoring in the easing but most analysts had expected it to occur after next Tuesday's RBA board meeting. The following is selection of economists' immediate reactions to the RBA announcement.
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"They like to surprise with the timing and to some extent they have done that today. The cut was fully expected and just about fully priced. I can now say with much more confidence than after previous rate cuts that this is likely to be the last one. Having said that, we would expect the current cash rate to be maintained right through the current financial year."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"The only oddity in the whole thing was the timing. Just about everbody has been expecting a rate cut in the very short term and the RBA has come through. Certainly with inflation dead in the water and unemployment still high there seems to be no reason not to cut rates."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:
"The cut was expected, but not today. They obviously don't see any reason to tie rate cuts to board meetings. There might be some attempt to price in another rate cut."
HANS KUNNEN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"The cash rate cut is welcome in the market. The economy will benefit from the move. The timing, although a week early, was within the time-frame expected from the market. We just now have to contemplate the RBA's next move. The rate cut will not affect inflation as global and domestic forces are keeping it in line."
JEFF OUGHTON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"They are conceding that growth is moderate ... There is a small chance that the economy will continue to run sub-potential here and, if wages pressure mitigates further and inflationary expectations continue to come down, you can't completely rule it (another rate cut) out .... But it's unlikely. The real issue is how quickly and how far rates will need to come up in '98 as the economy rebounds and as the flow-through of the lower currency feeds into underlying inflation...."
TONY MEER, ECONOMIST, DEUTCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"The timing was certainly a surprise and is a clear signal that the if the market tries to pick a day the bank will frustrate it. This move was fully priced in, but what's really interesting about the statement is how emphatic the bank is about the favourable inflation outlook. The comment that there was little risk of meeting capacity constraints over the next year or two even if growth were stronger than expected, is a very strong statement. It suggests the bank sees enough room for yet another easing, if not two."
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS:

"We think it is the right decision and my view is that this will be the last cut in this cycle. The bank itself will not rule out another cut, but at this point I would think another cut is highly unlikely now that we are half a percent under the Fed funds and with the likelihood that the U.S will tigthen some time in the next six months. I don't think they (RBA) have to look at it (interest rate movement) for another year."
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA RESEARCH INSTITUTE:

"The actual rate cut itself is no surprise. Now, the question is going to turn to will there be another. With the inflation outlook so good for at least the next two or three quarters the markets are certainly going to be speculating on another interest rate cut. My guess is this is probably going to be the floor for cash rates at 5.0 percent. Another rate cut would risk some substantial exchange rate weakness and that would translate to higher inflation, plus we are likely to see stronger economic signs over the second half of 1997."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"It was a well warranted rate cut, but they still managed to pick a day that's confused everybody. Forget about Reserve Bank board meetings from now on, it seems to be on significant pieces of data. And the significant data was clearly last week's inflation readings and average weekly earnings data, and the fact that while there are some signs of strength in the economy, it is still not accelerating fast enough. The issue now is because it is a fairly open-end statement, whether there is any potential for a further rate cut, and you have to say having read through it, you can't rule out the possibility."
GLENN MAGUIRE, ECONOMIST, SOCIETE GENERALE AUSTRALIA:

"The rate cut today was an appropriate adjustment to monetary policy. It is appropriate today as the market was pulling back from pricing in the fifth easing. The speculation on Friday's rate cut was as a result of the RBA underpinning the wages and inflation figures. Today the RBA validated market expectations. Inflation will continue to decline and we forecast that the December and March quarters will see an ultra low inflation rate."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
